explainers.assault: An assault is a stand-up fight against a line that is already set. The defender masses at the center and dares you to come dig them out; the attacker comes on from its own edge with no mines and no traps, just weight and aim. As the attacker, pick one point of the line and break it, because a force spread thin feeds itself to the guns piecemeal. As the defender, make every exchange cost more than it gains — the attacker has to come to you, and every turn they hesitate is a turn you spend shooting.
explainers.breakthrough: A breakthrough is a race, not a brawl. The attacker wins by punching a hole in the line and getting units out — the printed objectives say how many must exit off the defender's home edge — the far edge from you — before the defense closes ranks. As the attacker, do not stop to trade fire — every turn spent slugging is a turn the defense uses to close ranks. As the defender, you do not have to destroy the enemy; you have to stand in the road and make the crossing too expensive to finish.
explainers.defend: A Defend track is a holding action on a short, hard clock. The attacker has to lever the defenders off whatever they are protecting, usually the center, and fast — so expect the push to come heavy from the first turn. As the defender, deploy tight around the center and trade carefully — a third of your force arrives at the end of turn 1, and the fight can be lost before it gets there. As the attacker, commit early and hit one point of the line hard; a cautious approach runs the clock out and hands the defenders the track.
explainers.flank: A flank is about getting your weight onto the enemy's side before they can turn to face it. The attacker pins the defense in place with a third of its force, then swings the rest in from a short edge on turn 2. As the attacker, time the two arms to hit together — elements that arrive separately get beaten separately. As the defender, watch the short edges and keep something free to turn; your forward emplacements punish the attacker only if the rest of your line is not caught facing the wrong way.
explainers.meeting: A meeting engagement is a chance clash — neither side is dug in, and nobody brings traps or fixed defenses. Both forces enter on turn 1 from opposite edges, so the fight is usually decided by who seizes the center first and keeps formation while holding it. Push your weight forward as one body, because a force that arrives piecemeal is beaten piecemeal. Read the objectives before you commit; the only ground worth bleeding for is the ground that scores.
explainers.objective-raid: An objective raid is a smash-and-grab against the clock. The raiders have to reach the objective structures near the center, take what they came for, and carry it off their own edge; the garrison wins by keeping the raiders away from the structures and letting nothing leave the map. As the raider, make speed the plan — the longer you linger at the objective, the more of the defense concentrates on you. As the garrison, do not get pulled into chasing kills; a raider who leaves empty-handed is a raider you beat.
explainers.pursuit: A pursuit is about pinning, not chasing. Both forces enter from the same edge — the quarry first, with at least half its force slow, and the pursuer one turn behind at full speed. As the pursuer, get ahead of the slow half and cut the road instead of trailing the fast half; whatever exits the far edge is gone for good. As the quarry, screen with your fast units and keep the slow ones moving, because every turn a unit stands to fight is a turn it is not escaping.
explainers.pushback: A pushback is a fight against pressure from two directions at once. The attacker comes on from its own edge and across the long edges past the midline, with extra vehicle weight behind the push. As the defender, you deploy first and hold your ground: pick a line you can cover both ways, and refuse to be levered off it one flank at a time. As the attacker, make the two axes bite together — a defender allowed to face each one in turn will beat them both.
explainers.recon: A recon is about knowledge, not ground. Scanning rules are in effect, so information is the win condition — recon objectives are met by ending movement close to an enemy unit to identify it, or by getting and keeping eyes on the ground the objectives name, not by destroying things. As the attacker, use speed and cover to tag the enemy force and get clear, because a dead scout reports nothing. As the defender, deny them the information: keep your main force screened behind other units, destroy or drive off the scouts, and run out the clock.
explainers.retreat: A retreat is a fighting withdrawal, not a rout. The withdrawing side enters from the enemy's edge and has to fight the length of the map to escape off its own, with the pursuit arriving one turn behind. If you are withdrawing, keep the force moving — a unit that stands to fight usually stays for good; check your objectives for whether a crippled unit that limps off still counts. If you are pursuing, do not chase tails; get ahead of the column and force it to turn and fight where you choose.
explainers.strike: A strike is about the target, not the ground. Four identical structures stand near the center, and one of them is secretly the enemy headquarters; the attacker has to scan buildings to find it, then destroy it. As the attacker, use your split arrival (half your force on turn 1, the rest from a short edge on turn 2) to reach buildings the first wave cannot. As the defender, keep the raiders off the structures, and do not give the headquarters away by guarding it more heavily than the rest — every extra building they must scan costs them a turn they cannot spare.

contractVictory: This contract is won track by track at Scale {SCALE}. {EMPLOYER_NAME} counts it won if you win more tracks than you lose; anything less and {EMPLOYER_NAME} calls it a disappointment.

{EMPLOYER_NAME} pays track by track, but the final track is the one it remembers. End the contract on a win and the relationship outlives whatever came before; end it on a loss and that loss is the story it tells.

The contract is won track by track. Each track you win strengthens the employer's hold on the ground; win them all and the contract closes as a full success, and your command's name is worth more everywhere it is spoken.
{EMPLOYER_NAME} set one test for this contract: never let a loss stand. A lost track can be recovered by winning the track it forces, but a contract that ends on a loss is judged by that loss.

Pay lands track by track; the employer's judgment is tallied at the end. Across this Scale {SCALE} contract, {EMPLOYER_NAME} weighs objectives completed against objectives conceded; finish ahead on that tally and {EMPLOYER_NAME} judges the contract a success.

Both commands were hired to decide the same question. Pay lands track by track on both sides of it, but only one command leaves with its employer satisfied — and {EMPLOYER_NAME} judges by who holds the field when the last track is done.
Winning the fights is half the job: {EMPLOYER_NAME} counts this contract a success only if the tracks go your way and the thing it hired you to protect or take is still worth having when they do.
Each track's result sets the footing for the next — take the early ones and the late ones are fought on your terms; drop them and this contract becomes a climb back out, paid at the same rate.
The real measure of this contract is the opposition: end it with the opposition weaker than you found it, track by track, and {EMPLOYER_NAME} will call the money well spent.

This contract runs its full length whatever the early tracks bring, and {EMPLOYER_NAME} judges the command that finishes it — a force still fit to fight at the end is worth more than one that burned itself winning.
behindScenes: The {TARGET_FACTION} commitment on {WORLD} is heavier than {EMPLOYER_NAME} admits in the brief — play the opposition as a force fighting for keeps from the first turn. The root track's result drives the branch: a win routes to the track that presses the advantage, a loss to the track that recovers it. Read each fork's consequence line at resolve so the table feels the campaign move.

What {EMPLOYER_NAME} calls a limited action is really a probe. {TARGET_FACTION_THE} is testing how hard {WORLD} is to take, and the root track is the test. Stopped cold, the opposition pulls back and the tree turns to running them down; if it breaks through, it presses the real objective and the later tracks fight over that. Do not soften the FAILURE branch — it is a genuine fallback, and the contract can still be saved from it.

{TARGET_FACTION_THE} is on {WORLD} for one prize, and the early tracks only position the fight around it. Route the tree by the printed forks: each consequence line tells you what the next track is and why. Keep the prize in view whichever branch runs — it is what the final track settles.

The part {EMPLOYER_NAME} left out of the brief: its own strength on {WORLD} is thinner than it claims, and there is no cavalry behind the players' command. If the root track is lost, run the FAILURE branch with real weight — the opposition smells the weakness and presses. Wins route forward through the printed forks; either path closes the contract when the last track resolves.

Play the {TARGET_FACTION} commander as a professional with a schedule, not a grudge. The force on {WORLD} has somewhere else to be, and every track it loses tightens that clock — expect it to press hard early and cut its losses late. The root result drives the branch; settle the tally and the reputation consequences when the intensity is spent.

Both sides are being used. {EMPLOYER_NAME} wants {TARGET_FACTION_THE} bled on {WORLD} at a mercenary's price, and the opposition's paymaster wants the same in reverse — neither backer commits its own line troops if it can help it. Run the tree by the printed forks and let the players work that out on their own; it lands harder discovered than told.

Someone on {EMPLOYER_NAME}'s staff is selling the players' movement schedule, and the opposition's early deployments should show it — let the enemy be waiting once, plainly, on the root track. Whether the leak is ever found is the GM's call; the selling stops the moment the opposition decides the intelligence is no longer worth the price.

The people of {WORLD} have outlasted three garrisons and expect to outlast this one — play the locals as courteous, unhelpful, and a step ahead of both sides' patrols. Any track fought carelessly around them turns the countryside quietly hostile: guides mislead, reports dry up, and the opposition starts hearing about the players' movements first.

{TARGET_FACTION_THE} is fighting at the end of a supply line it cannot afford, and every track it loses stretches it thinner. Let the opposition open aggressive and grow careful: by the later tracks it husbands ammunition, refuses attrition, and breaks off fights a fresh force would have finished. If the players read the change and press the tempo, reward them for it.

The contract is real but the timetable is not: {EMPLOYER_NAME} needs this fight loud and visible exactly now, as cover for a move it is making somewhere else entirely. Nothing on {WORLD} has to change hands for the employer to get what it paid for — which is why the terms are generous and the oversight is thin. The players are the diversion; whether they ever learn it is up to the table.

complications.name: Ash on the Wind
complications.effect: Volcanic ash hangs over the field for the whole battle. All weapon attacks beyond short range suffer +1 to-hit, and every 'Mech adds 1 extra heat in any turn it runs or jumps.

complications.name: Squall Front
complications.effect: A storm line covers the map from turn 4 to the end of the battle: all weapon attacks take +1 to-hit, no unit may jump, and clear hexes cost 1 extra MP as the ground softens.

complications.name: Low Ceiling
complications.effect: Cloud sits at rooftop height. Aerospace units may not operate, VTOLs must fly at treetop height (elevation 1 or lower) for the whole battle, and any reinforcement slated to arrive by air instead walks on from its own home edge one turn late.

complications.name: Thin Air Plateau
complications.effect: The field sits above 4,000 meters. Every 'Mech dissipates 2 fewer heat each turn than its heat sinks allow, and VTOLs reduce both cruise and flank speed by 2.

complications.name: Furnace Season
complications.effect: Midday on {WORLD} is hotter than any cockpit rating. All 'Mechs add 2 heat at the end of any turn they moved, and depth 1 water hexes count as rough terrain — the beds are baked dry.

complications.name: Black Ice Morning
complications.effect: Overnight frost has glazed every road and paved hex. A unit entering one at running speed must pass a Piloting Skill Roll or fall; a vehicle that fails instead skids one hex forward and ends its movement.

complications.name: Grit in the Works
complications.effect: Wind-driven grit fouls actuators and intakes. At the end of each turn, roll 1d6 for every unit that ran or jumped; on a 1 it takes one critical-hit roll against a random location.

complications.name: Levee Failure
complications.effect: An upstream levee gives way on turn 3. From turn 4 onward every hex adjacent to a water hex becomes depth 1 water, and a unit standing in one when it floods must pass a Piloting Skill Roll or fall.

complications.name: Early Dark
complications.effect: The fight runs into local night. From turn 6 onward all weapon attacks suffer +2 to-hit unless the firer has a searchlight trained on its target or an active probe in range.

complications.name: Guns Beyond the Ridge
complications.effect: Off-map artillery supports the opposition. Once per battle, at the start of a turn, the GM places a strike on any hex an enemy unit can see; every unit in or adjacent to it takes 10 damage in 5-point groups.

complications.name: Follow-On Lance
complications.effect: A fresh opposition lance is closer than the brief admitted. At the end of turn 5, roll 1d6; on 4+ a formation roughly the weight of one of the players' lances enters on a map edge of the GM's choice and joins the opposition.

complications.name: Quiet Minefields
complications.effect: The approaches were seeded weeks ago. Before deployment the GM secretly notes three hexes; the first unit to enter each one takes 10 damage to the legs or motive system and must pass a Piloting Skill Roll or fall.

complications.name: Marksman on Overwatch
complications.effect: A veteran gunner is working the field for the opposition. Each turn, after all movement, the GM picks one enemy unit; it treats its Gunnery skill as 1 better for its attacks that turn.

complications.name: Jamming Carpet
complications.effect: Hostile electronic warfare blankets the map. Player units may not share targeting data or use indirect fire, and their probes and advanced sensors are useless beyond 3 hexes.

complications.name: Prepared Countermoves
complications.effect: The enemy commander drilled for exactly this fight. The opposition wins all initiative ties, and once per battle it may interrupt the players' movement to move one of its own units first.

complications.name: Satchel Teams
complications.effect: Anti-'Mech infantry wait in the built-up area. The first time a player 'Mech ends its movement adjacent to a building, a hidden platoon attacks its legs with satchel charges for 2d6 damage (one leg, rolled randomly, applied as one group), then is placed on the map.

complications.name: Strafing Run
complications.effect: The opposition has one fighter on call. Once per battle the GM draws a line of 5 adjacent hexes; every unit under it takes 5 damage in one group, and the aircraft cannot be engaged and does not return.

complications.name: Feigned Rout
complications.effect: If the opposition falls below half its starting units it breaks for its home edge in apparent disorder. Two turns later a fresh pair of enemy units enters that same edge, and any enemy unit that withdrew returns with them.

complications.name: No Quarter Asked
complications.effect: The opposition is past caring about survival. Enemy units never withdraw and never eject, and every crippled enemy machine spends its last turns ramming or firing on the nearest player unit.

complications.name: Short Magazines
complications.effect: Resupply never arrived. Every player unit begins the battle with half its normal ammunition per ammunition-fed weapon, rounded down; energy weapons are unaffected.

complications.name: Deferred Maintenance
complications.effect: The command has outrun its technicians. Before deployment, roll 1d6 for each player unit; on a 1 that unit starts the fight with one critical hit already applied to a randomly rolled location.

complications.name: Harvest Crews Afield
complications.effect: Civilian crews are still working the field. The GM places three harvester vehicles in open hexes, each moving 2 hexes toward the nearest edge every turn; no one may target them, and stray damage that destroys one costs the responsible side 50 victory points.

complications.name: Orders Mid-Fight
complications.effect: {EMPLOYER} amends the mission over the command channel. At the start of turn 4 the GM names one map edge; at least one player unit must end the battle within 3 hexes of that edge or the opposition gains 50 victory points.

complications.name: Volunteers Underfoot
complications.effect: A local militia platoon insists on joining. It deploys with the players and moves as the GM directs; on any turn it takes fire, roll 1d6 — on 1-2 it routs toward the nearest edge, blocking every hex it crosses.

complications.name: A Truce at Noon
complications.effect: Diplomats are close to a local ceasefire. The battle ends at the close of turn 10 regardless of the situation on the ground, and any objective not achieved by then is lost.

complications.name: Wayward Resupply
complications.effect: A supply pod comes down in the wrong grid. The GM places a cache in a random hex on the map's centerline; the first unit to end its movement there may refill one empty ammunition bin or shed 1d6 heat, and the cache then expires.

complications.name: Broadcast Live
complications.effect: A news crew is transmitting from a marked hilltop hex. Neither side may attack that hex, and whichever side has a unit in or adjacent to it when the battle ends gains 50 victory points as the coverage leads their way.

complications.name: Mutiny Rumors
complications.effect: Half the opposition has not been paid this quarter. From turn 6 onward, roll 1d6 at the start of each turn; on a 6 one enemy unit of the GM's choice powers down and takes no further part in the fight.

complications.name: Condemned Blocks
complications.effect: The district's buildings are decades past their rating. Any building hex that takes 10 or more damage in one turn collapses at once, and units inside or adjacent take 15 falling-debris damage in 5-point groups.

complications.name: Tinder Ground
complications.effect: The vegetation is a season past dry. Any woods hex hit by an energy weapon catches fire on 8+ on 2d6; fires spread one hex downwind each turn (the GM sets a wind direction at setup) and fill their hexes with sight-blocking smoke.

complications.name: Live Power Trunks
complications.effect: Buried power trunks cross the field, with four junction hexes marked at setup. A unit ending its movement in one takes 5 electrical damage, and a 'Mech must also pass a Piloting Skill Roll or fall.

complications.name: Magnetic Lode
complications.effect: Iron-heavy ground blinds instruments across the whole map. Sensors and probes do not function, all identification is visual, and hidden units stay hidden until they move or fire.

complications.name: Bottomless Mud
complications.effect: Spring melt has turned the low ground to slurry. Clear hexes at the map's lowest elevation cost 1 extra MP to enter, and a 'Mech that falls in one needs a full turn of movement to regain its feet.

complications.name: Loose Scree Slopes
complications.effect: The high ground is rotten rock. A unit entering a hex at elevation 2 or higher at running speed must pass a Piloting Skill Roll or slide one level down and end its movement prone.

complications.name: Tremor Swarms
complications.effect: Seismic tremors run under the field all day. At the start of each turn roll 2d6; on 11 or higher every standing 'Mech must pass a Piloting Skill Roll or fall, and every building hex takes 5 structural damage.

complications.name: One Span Standing
complications.effect: A single bridge crosses the watercourse splitting the map. It bears 60 tons and has CF 60; if it drops, the only crossings left are depth 2 water hexes, and anything that cannot wade them fights on its own bank.
